name: Zheng-Dao Bioelectric Sensorium Graft — 'The Cartographer'
description:
The Cartographer is a proprioceptive and spatial-sensing augmentation that expands the user's awareness of their own body and immediate environment into a continuous, real-time three-dimensional model maintained in a dedicated neural processing partition. The system combines a dense mesh of pressure and position sensors embedded beneath the skin across the body's full surface area with a short-range electromagnetic field emitter anchored at the sternum that reads the return signature of nearby objects and surfaces. This data is synthesized by Zheng-Dao's spatial processing co-processor — a rice-grain implant seated against the cerebellum — into a proprioceptive map that the user experiences as a kind of ambient spatial knowing: a detailed, constantly updated sense of exactly where their body is in space and exactly what is within approximately four meters of them.

The subjective experience of the Cartographer is famously difficult to describe to non-users. It is not vision — the electromagnetic sense does not produce images. Users consistently describe it as a tactile awareness extended beyond the skin, as though the body's sense of its own boundaries has expanded to include the surrounding volume. In darkness, in smoke, in complete sensory deprivation, a Cartographer user retains a precise, granular model of their immediate environment. Zheng-Dao's research documentation notes that long-term users frequently develop what the company calls 'spatial fluency' — an unconscious, high-speed exploitation of the spatial model that manifests as uncanny movement precision, an ability to navigate complex environments at speed without visible hesitation or error.

The Cartographer was originally developed as a clinical tool for individuals with severe proprioceptive disorders, and Zheng-Dao still markets it in that context as a licensed medical device. Its adoption by the tactical community came later, driven by operators working in environments where visual and electronic sensing is compromised. The system is notably difficult to jam or spoof: the electromagnetic emitter operates on a frequency-hopping protocol across a range that most tactical jammers don't cover, and the skin-surface sensor mesh has no external signal to intercept.

cultural_context: Within Zheng-Dao's own research community, the Cartographer is regarded as one of the company's most elegant pieces of bioelectric engineering — a system that expands human sense rather than replacing it, which aligns with Zheng-Dao's stated philosophy of 'augmentation as extension, not substitution.' In the broader culture of Meridian 88, Cartographer users are sometimes identified by behavioral tells: they tend to move with unusual precision in tight spaces, rarely bump into things, and have a habit of positioning themselves in rooms with their backs to open space, an instinct cultivated by the ambient rear-awareness the system provides. Among those who can't afford it, the Cartographer has a reputation as a rich person's augmentation — medically licensed, expensively installed, and associated with the kind of person who has a surgeon on retainer.
known_users: Tactical operatives working in electronic blackout conditions
Individuals with clinical proprioceptive disorders (licensed medical use)
Underground martial artists and fighting circuit competitors
Infiltration specialists working in smoke and darkness
story_hooks: A Cartographer user is the key witness to a killing that happened in complete darkness. They know exactly where everyone in that room was. The problem is that what they sensed contradicts the official account, and someone very powerful needs that account to stand.

Zheng-Dao's clinical database of Cartographer users — including their spatial behavioral profiles — has been stolen. The data could be used to identify and locate specific individuals based on how they move through documented environments.

A player character begins experiencing phantom spatial data — the Cartographer is mapping spaces they're not in, showing them rooms, corridors, environments that don't match their location. The co-processor is receiving someone else's spatial feed.

An assassin with a Cartographer has been operating in a district with no functional lighting — they've been using the power grid outages as cover. The only way to find them is to understand how they're navigating.
